title: Sean Duffy in the Real World
author: @NewYorker
content:
I am a sucker for a travel show—if it involves people going to a place and doing a thing, count me in. My current favorites include the BBC’s “Race Across the World,” in which the scenery is usually the star—last season, sweeping shots of frozen mountain vistas had me itching to book a trip to Mongolia—and “Jet Lag: The Game,” a web series that a friend of a friend got me very, very into, in which three charming American nerds and a rotating guest player turn the world into the setting for a real-life board game, or similar. Here, the scenery is less the star than the hosts and the silly challenges they take on. In one recent season, the players had to “claim” as many adjacent U.S. states as possible by, for example, sculpting a butter animal (in Iowa), drinking at a bourbon distillery (in Kentucky), or doing time-zone trivia at a Margaritaville (in any state with a Margaritaville). It is, after all, five o’clock somewhere.

You can imagine my excitement, then, when I learned about a forthcoming YouTube offering called “The Great American Road Trip.” This one promised not only travel-show vibes but, perhaps, a sprinkling of reality TV, another guilty pleasure of mine. One of the hosts, Sean Duffy, appeared, back in 1997, on the sixth season of “The Real World,” the MTV staple in which bright young things from varied backgrounds moved in together, in this case in Boston; his memorable moments included calling one castmate a bitch and dry-humping another before gyrating with a pool cue. The new show’s other host, Rachel Campos, also appeared on a season of “The Real World”; later, she and Duffy met on a spinoff, “Road Rules” (more of the same, but on a road trip), got married, and had nine children. Campos-Duffy is now a host on Fox News; Duffy, who has hosted on Fox Business and served as a congressman from Wisconsin, is currently Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary. Indeed, it was in this capacity that he launched “The Great American Road Trip,” with a promise to inspire other families to hit the road in honor of the country’s Semiquincentennial. “Our motto is ‘To love America is to see America,’ ” Duffy said, on Fox, in May. Campos-Duffy, sitting next to him, added that, in our “PornHub world,” the show would be “really wholesome, good family stuff.” A trailer promised as much—but also some drama.

By the time Duffy spoke about it on Fox, “The Great American Road Trip” was more or less in the can, and he said that episodes would drop in June, perhaps in time for the peak of the Semiquincentennial celebrations and summer travel season. But June brought no show, and neither did July. Meanwhile, controversy swirled around the initiative. Some critics attacked it as tone-deaf, given the war in Iran and the attendant, spiralling gas prices. (Rolling Stone calculated that a Duffy-style trip this summer might cost upward of a thousand dollars in fuel alone.) Others highlighted ethical concerns: the show was funded by a namesake nonprofit that cut sponsorship deals with various major companies—the aerospace giant Boeing, the construction provider CRH, the autonomous-driving service Waymo—that fall within Duffy’s regulatory purview. The Transportation Department insisted that this was all above board, claiming, among other things, that the road trip was official business and that Duffy had folded in relevant work meetings. After the trailer met with a withering reaction, Duffy took aim at a “radical, miserable left” that, he said, didn’t like what he was doing because “it’s too wholesome. It’s too patriotic. It’s too joyful.” During a contentious hearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee, Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington, suggested that the whole endeavor stank. Duffy shot back, “Don’t you want to celebrate America? Let’s celebrate this country. It’s our birthday.”

On Wednesday, “The Great American Road Trip” finally landed on YouTube, in six episodes of a half hour or so each. (Technically, it should have been called “The Great American Road Trips”; as officials were keen to point out, it was filmed in installments over a period of months.) At long last, it was time to tune out the naysayers and joy haters, and judge the show on the only terms that matter for a product of the Trump Administration: whether or not it’s good TV.

During Trump’s first term, in particular, the President couldn’t pass a bowel movement without pundits declaring it “made for TV.” More often than not, I found this unbearably annoying—part of a persistent media inclination to grade the optics of the things that Trump did rather than, well, the things that Trump did. But I also felt annoyance at critics who seemed to see any mention of TV in politics as tantamount to dumbing down. TV, after all, can be very good!

Embarking on “The Great American Road Trip,” I quickly started to fear that it was not very good. The first episode—a trip to see Trump at the White House, then on to Philadelphia to learn about the Liberty Bell, meet a Benjamin Franklin impersonator, and race up the “Rocky” steps—has the feel of a promotional video that one might watch in the back of a cab. Patrick—one of the Duffys’ kids, a few of whom have clearly inherited their parents’ screen chops and brightened up the show considerably—matched my energy when a producer asked if he found it cool to visit the White House, and he replied that “it’s kind of boring, because you’re just sitting there watching your parents talk.” (“What’s so good about having cheese and steak?” Patrick asks later. “You can make that at home.”)

If Episode 1 put me to sleep, Episode 2 quickly jolted me awake. Before the Duffys even leave for their destination—Boston, this time—we learn that their daughter Paloma is applying to colleges, including Harvard, which, she says, would be hard to turn down. “Well, me and Mom can say no,” Duffy replies. Cue tense music and a disquisition on the importance of Catholicism to Duffy père and mère, who are concerned that Harvard has perfected how to take “good young girls” and “corrupt their minds.” Paloma doesn’t think that this is very open-minded, and the argument continues in the car. Eventually, both are parked—Duffy has taken the kids to see the firehouse that he once inhabited on “The Real World,” where they are welcomed in by Montana, the castmate he dry-humped. But the college plot soon recommences, and the Duffys eventually speak with a Harvard chaplain who, to some extent, is able to allay their anxieties about brainwashing. (“There is a refuge, it appears, in the Catholic Church” at Harvard, Duffy reflects. Campos-Duffy admits, “I didn’t wanna like the situation as much as I did.”) By this point, I was getting a little worried about the separation of church and state. Then I remembered, with relief, that the series was funded by corporate sponsors.

There is more drama in Episode 3 (Wyoming and Montana—the state, not the castmate): the Duffys’ eldest daughter, Evita, and her husband, Michael, who has amazing eyebrows and is currently vying for Duffy’s old congressional seat, invite an ultrasound technician to their cabin to find out the sex of their unborn child; meanwhile, Patrick has to go to the hospital after collapsing with visibly agonizing stomach pain that doctors think might be appendicitis. Happily, it turns out to be constipation, much to the amusement of the rest of the family. (“I don’t want to embarrass him,” one of his sisters says, long after that horse had bolted.) The remaining episodes—a trip to Charleston, with a detour to a Boeing plant; a trip to Texas, with a detour to a CRH subsidiary; a trip to Arizona, with a ride in a Waymo—mostly settle back into the tedium of Episode 1. Perhaps most upsetting for me, the show, as a whole, never seems to figure out whether it is primarily travel or reality, or whether the scenery or the people should be the star. The creators could have done more to bring out the gorgeous landscapes that the Duffys visited; they could, at least, have fed us some dumb challenges, with alcohol or not. Ultimately, I came away with no idea who the show is supposed to be for, although, if its paltry early view count is any guide, the answer might be “no one.”

A few months ago, in anticipation of the show’s release, I watched some old episodes of “The Real World” to get in the spirit. They were extremely dated. They were also vastly more interesting than “The Great American Road Trip” would prove to be. Duffy, for his part, came across as a real jerk at times, but surprisingly charming at others, with a half-nerd, half-jock mien—sweepy hair, big glasses, a megawatt smile—that put me in mind of a Wisconsin Sam Seaborn. (Call it “The Midwest Wing.”) According to the Times, Duffy told his “Real World” castmates that he aspired to be President one day, and “The Great American Road Trip” certainly had me wondering whether the point was to promote American travel or Duffy himself. For the record, Duffy has strongly disclaimed any interest in the White House, which is, after all, just a bunch of boring grownups talking. His show—in which he does beautiful family things with his beautiful family—does feel like a shop window, though. And, even if it isn’t, it’s an interesting thought experiment to consider whether, in this media moment, it would work as one.

It’s tempting to look at Duffy’s political ascent—and Trump’s, of course—and reflect on the surprising cultural sticking power of turn-of-the-millennium-style reality TV. And so, I will. The Trump Presidency likely wouldn’t have been possible without “The Apprentice.” Duffy’s rise has been less meteoric, but his launchpad, if anything, was an even purer distillation of the genre; as my colleague Emily Nussbaum has written, “The Real World” pioneered many of reality TV’s modern tropes—the cast of strangers, the apartment as set, the confessional interviews—and cultivated a viewership that no longer saw reality TV as a “crummy stopgap” for scripted fare but the thing to watch. When I revisited the show earlier this summer, it seemed a particularly propitious moment to assert the ongoing influence of reality TV, not least in politics. Spencer Pratt, the villain from “The Hills,” was running for mayor of Los Angeles, depicting the city as a hellhole and attracting reams of media coverage. Luke Gulbranson (“Summer House”) was running for a (year-round) U.S. House seat in Minnesota. Mark Moran (“FBoy Island”) was running for Senate in Virginia.

The moment no longer seems so propitious. Moran dropped out; Gulbranson lost, as, more significantly, did Pratt, occasioning some hand-wringing about whether his supposed surge had ever been real to begin with. (In fairness, almost nothing is more reality-TV than that.) More broadly, the genre’s future, at least as conventional TV, is in doubt, in this era of social media, podcasts, and YouTube. And yet, arguably, this array has made everything into reality TV and given everyone the tools to be a star; certainly, the genre’s codes—chiefly, its obsessions with conflict and with evaluating people’s authenticity—are baked into our modern media culture. Perhaps the most reality-TV moment of the past week came when the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff mocked Trump for flying around on his plane with “Natalie,” a winking reference to a young aide who is known for her particularly obsequious devotion to the President—and as the “human printer,” because she follows him around feeding him digital content in hard-copy form. The footage was endlessly clipped and debated. Trump responded by likening Ossoff to Pee-wee Herman. The White House communications director called him “the biggest cuck loser in politics.” (Ossoff, not Herman.)

It was certainly the most reality-TV moment of the past week to involve a politician’s travel schedule. Ironically, given his impeccable credentials, Duffy’s show didn’t come close: to the extent that it trades in “authenticity,” it is of the performative, Americana-drenched variety that the word has come to signify in politics, despite bearing little relationship to what’s real; nor does the show serve up any conflict. (Aside from the Harvard row, anyway, and even that ends happily. Spoiler ahead! Paloma is pleased to be accepted to the University of Chicago.) Throughout his political career, Duffy has seemed ambivalent about his reality roots, at times dismissing them as irrelevant, and at others leaning in, as he does, explicitly, in the Boston episode of “The Great American Road Trip,” and, implicitly, in the show’s over-all orientation. He has pushed back on the idea that the show is reality TV, but not all that convincingly—you can take the star out of reality, but not reality out of the star. Maybe, if he’d more successfully kept his distance, he could just have made a great travel show—something less “Real World” and more “real world.”

Duffy, of course, might believe that this is exactly what he did. Touting the series on X, he wrote, “America isn’t something you can understand through a phone screen. You have to get out and see it.” This is fair. If his show makes a compelling case for anything, it’s less screen time. ♦

title: "The lines between redemption and revenge will blur", promises Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2's latest trailer as the series locks in a late October release
author: Mark Warren
content:
Edgerunning closer

Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2, the second series of the anime CD Projekt Red and Netflix grafted onto the former's cyberverse following Cyberpunk 2077's release, will premiere on October 20th. Having previously revealed the four new Night City dwellers its plot will be following, the show's creators have now put out another trailer teasing the tale of "revenge and redemption" in store.

The thing that's stuck out to me about the new teaser, which you can watch above, is that it appears to split the four leads off into two pairs. Veteran edgerunner Weak Kingsley, the bloke in the grey coat, looks to have been tasked with helping chromed-up Talia Yang escape the corpo life before it chews her up and spits her out, all while confronting his own past demons as he adjusts to life without cyberware. Meanwhile, nomad netrunner D's escaped a fire that wiped out his clan and ends up meeting Roman Carax, the kid with the camcorder keen to document the city's stories.

From there, there's a lot of shooting and shouting that all four look to have a hand in and some creepy chat about D being "a weapon made out of people". All in all, the series looks like a shot of action and arguably over-the-top emotional drama right to your frontal lobe. I'm keen to give it more of a chance to win me over than I did the first series, especially now I know it'll be coming around the time most games aside from Call of Duty run for the hills to avoid doing anything major around GTA 6's console launch. I love Cyberpunk as a game, though a lot of that comes from being able to explore Night City myself, but I think I could be persuaded to dig the anime with a bit more exposure.

Regardless, I'm pretty sure the legions of folks who loved the first series will be tempted into taking on another playthrough of V's story once they've binged Edgerunners 2.

title: Over the Hill, SnowRunner's hippie off-roading cousin from the Art of Rally devs, gets an October release date
author: Mark Warren
content:
Start packing your camping supplies

Fire up the Landy! Over the Hill, Funselektor and Strelka Games' off-roader which takes the hardcore trail-running you get in a sim like SnowRunner and sands off the edges a bit to make for more chill countryside-roaming, finally has a release date. It's set to motor onto the scene in October, following a Steam Next Fest demo which I dug.

October 14th is the exact date Over the Hill will trundle onto Steam in full, meaning it'll rock up not long after Star Wars: Galactic Racer and will have to fight September castoff Valor Mortis (not that the latter two bear many similarities).

If you missed my impressions of its Next Fest demo in June, Over the Hill's part chummy drive through nature on your own or with up to three co-op mates, part mischievous trickster that's trying to lull you into a false sense of security so it can cackle at your broken down misfortune when you accidentally seize your engine trying to ford a river that's too deep or roll into some trees at such an angle that you can't easily get your jeep back on its wheels.

Exploration and wildlife-spotting across open wilderness maps is the name of the game, hunting for the likes of cabins to stay in, upgrades for your customisable ride, and the likes of challenging off-road trails that'll test your driving and winching skills. As with Funselektor's previous works like Art of Rally and Absolute Drift, it mixes minimalistic visual vibes and calm atmosphere with mechanics still capable of biting you if you relax too much and start to get careless.

I've had my eye on it for ages, so will almost certainly don my cargo shorts to give it a go in some form around release. If you like the look of it, you can wishlist it on Steam.

title: Take-Two lost $2.8 billion in market cap after GTA 6 leaks—but what's more shocking to me is it probably barely felt it
author: Harvey Randall
content:
One of the biggest stories this week has been of the enigmatic, self-described consumer hero Cyberleek, who's also using this whole debacle as a way to advertise and pay for their cryptocurrency. Which is probably fine and normal and not at all a concerning spectre lingering around one of the biggest games of the year.

Anyway, you'd think Take-Two and Strauss Zelnick might be feeling hot under the collar about all of this, and you'd be partially right. As spotted by Insider Gaming, Take-Two's market price (the price of one share) was around $248 before the leaks. Fast-forward a couple of days, and that same market price dropped to a low of $233.

This hit Take-Two's market cap (share price, times the amount of shares) to the tune of billions—around $2.83 billion in two days. An astronomical amount of money by any stretch of the imagination, a huge devaluation that's… actually not even much of a sweat, really.

See, Take-Two's overall market cap was still over $43 billion and, by virtue of how stock markets tend to shift and fluctuate, not even that much of a rare occurrence. On August 6, the market price dropped to a measly $229, for instance, before spiking back up to $242 the next day.

And while the overall market price between August 18 and 20 does trend downwards, it's already rising back up. At the time of writing, said market price has recovered to $241, with the market cap rising from that $43 billion total to almost $44.9 billion—just $1 billion within its previous number.

Look, while I don't think anyone at Take-Two's exactly happy to be losing a couple billion dollars in market cap to some guy peddling cryptocurrency with a full copy of their next big thing, what feels more noteworthy is the fact that a leak of this scale has mostly just pinged off the videogame giant's armour.

It's a humbling reminder of the sheer amount of money that gets poured into videogames at this scale—humbling or perhaps distressing, given the size of the industry tracks precious little to its security.

Harvey's history with games started when he first begged his parents for a World of Warcraft subscription aged 12, though he's since been cursed with Final Fantasy 14-brain and a huge crush on G'raha Tia. He made his start as a freelancer, writing for websites like Techradar, The Escapist, Dicebreaker, The Gamer, Into the Spine—and of course, PC Gamer. He'll sink his teeth into anything that looks interesting, though he has a soft spot for RPGs, soulslikes, roguelikes, deckbuilders, MMOs, and weird indie titles. He also plays a shelf load of TTRPGs in his offline time. Don't ask him what his favourite system is, he has too many.

title: Limited edition green see-through Xbox Series X reportedly costs as much as a PS5 Pro, and releases on Black Friday
author: Robert Purchese
content:
Master sheesh.

That fancy green see-through Xbox Series X - a limited edition creation for Xbox's 25th anniversary - reportedly releases on Black Friday and costs as much as a PS5 Pro.

The information comes from French website Dealabs' consistently reliable leaker billbil-kun, who claims the Xbox Series X25 Limited Edition - as Microsoft is calling it - releases 27th November priced €899.99 (or an estimated $899.99). At that price it's €100 more than a standard 1TB Xbox Series X with a disc drive and, as noted, the same price as PS5 Pro in Europe.

No UK equivalent pricing has been revealed, but a PS5 Pro costs £789.99 here so perhaps it'll be similarly priced. If it is, that would make the limited edition Xbox at least £100 more than the standard disc-drive Series X, which is priced £669.99. (The disc-drive comparison is appropriate because the limited edition Xbox Series X has one.)

Why is it so expensive? Presumably because it has a translucent murky-Xbox-green case, meaning you can peer inside at its techno-innards. It also comes with a special Xbox controller which has been given the same treatment: you can see inside its body. The Xbox Series X25 Limited Edition was unveiled at Microsoft's Xbox Games Showcase earlier this summer. We've asked Xbox for comment.

Since it was revealed, much has happened. The entire Xbox division has been rocked by wide-ranging restructuring, which has left 1600 people without a job already, and will leave a further 1600 people without jobs by next summer. It's restructuring that's resulted in first-party studios splitting from Xbox, as well as downsized studios. All this has affected game development and, understandably, staff morale. Protests continue to be organised in response.

Microsoft also substantially raised the prices of its Xbox consoles earlier this year, boosting the cheapest Xbox Series S from £300 to £430, and the disc-drive Xbox Series X from £500 to £670. The primary reason for this is the ongoing memory and storage component shortage around the world - a scarcity created by huge AI datacenter demand for the same things.

Xbox boss Asha Sharma has already warned that the component pricing crisis will continue, and that "we expect another doubling by the fall of 2027". This will affect pricing and availability of Xbox's next-gen Project Helix machine, she's said, and Microsoft is exploring "radically different business models" related to selling Xbox consoles because of it.

title: Worm Munch Matters
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
“Sound is a tangible way of connecting to aspects of nature that are hidden from humans. The deep ocean, the dark night, and now the dense earth beneath our feet,” writes Ella Browning. And you can hear underground for yourself in the fascinating recordings she includes in her essay on earthworm “munching.” In this emerging field of soil ecoacoustics, researchers—including Browning—are finding links between ecosystem recovery and the character of underground soundscapes. Healthy soil literally sounds different. This piece will change how you view the ground beneath your feet.

A core principle of ecoacoustics is that complexly noisy natural places are healthier natural places. This means that it’s not just the volume of noise, but the diversity of sound that indicates habitat health. The dawn chorus in an intact Bornean tropical forest is magical in its complexity, especially if you’re lucky to experience it mixed in with the whoops of a troop of gibbons swinging through overhead, as I was during a visit in 2019.

In contrast, cities are generally not ecologically healthy and, while they are incredibly noisy places, they are filled with the harsh, more monotonous sounds of car engines and other machines, and often little biotic sound. Soundscapes dominated by anthropogenic sounds have been linked to poor mental health in people, whereas the opposite has been found for natural sounds like birdsong or forest soundscapes.

title: Even Mussels Get Scared
content:
Predators can have big impacts on the landscape, and not just by doing what they do best—killing and eating their prey. The mere presence of a predator can alter the behavior of animals further down the food chain, causing cascading changes to the ecosystem. It’s a phenomenon known as the “ecology of fear,” and according to a new study published in the Journal of Helminthology, even the lowly mussel lives in fear of the tiniest predators.     

Featured Video

Marine biologists from Denmark’s Aarhus University put blue mussels (the same ones you might cook up with white wine, garlic, and linguini) in a tank with one of its most common micropredators, the parasitic flatworm Himasthla elongata. These tiny worms enter the mussels through the bivalve’s inhalant siphon, which they use to suck in water and filter out the algae they feed on. In the presence of the worm, the mussels narrowed their tubes, reducing their filtering activity by more than a third. When the team introduced a second species of parasitic flatworm (Renicola roscovita), filtration fell by more than half.

In the next experiment, the researchers put the mussels in a tank with chemical signals taken from the common periwinkle. These harmless marine snails don’t pose any direct threat to the mussels, but they are important hosts for H. elongata. Surprisingly, the mussels responded the same way, trimming their filtration activity by 42 percent. 

Read more: “Mussels Are Devastating a Unique Ecosystem”

“The snail itself doesn’t harm the mussel, but its presence can be a sign that parasites are nearby,” study author Pernille Kibak said in a statement. “It may almost work like a warning sign in the water: There is reason to be on your guard.”

Still, the researchers aren’t sure which chemical cues the mussels are responding to—introducing compounds from both infected and uninfected periwinkles had the same effect. Snail juice in general, it seems, is enough to make a mussel clam up.

According to the team, these findings could have important ecological implications. A single blue mussel can filter over 25 gallons of water a day, and mussel banks can contain millions of them. If they get spooked and turn off their filtration en masse, it could lead to overgrowths of algae, reduced nutrient cycling, and murky waters that may become inhospitable to other critters. Additionally, cooler waters tend to kill parasites off, so this dynamic could present a problem as warming oceans become more flatworm-friendly.

“That’s what makes this response so interesting,” Kibak said. “We’re looking at something that happens in an individual mussel, but because blue mussels play such an important role in coastal ecosystems, even small changes in their behavior could potentially matter on a much larger scale.”

And all from a tiny little worm.

title: “Saint Paul”
author: @NewYorker
content:
August 17, 2026

All my friends have their gods & their heavens& their plans on how to get there. They forfeit sexfor Lent, pork for life, they light incense, they lightcandles, they offer fruit to the dead.Is this the right time to confess that once I bit a boyfor calling me a Buddhist? Never mind I was six& did not know what Buddhist meant,never mind we were inside a Buddhist temple.For so long, I thought god was played by a rotating castof my dead. For so long, god was a boy with a ring of keyson his belt loop. I never had as much faith as I did then,but I never talked to god as much as I do now—nowthat my want is just the want of birds. At some point,someone invited me to Easter, then to Seder, then to Eid& for a night I talked to Andrew’s god, & for a night Italked to Sam’s god. I talked to Saf’s god. I was a wick litby any god that wandered by—an appetite primedfor the miracles of others. & then Paul got sick& then got better, & I said thank you thank you.Paul & I are from a city first named after a bootlegger& then renamed after a saint & when he died,I caught a flight to a city only he knew, where the humidityflattened the pleats I’d ironed into my pants.All my life, I’ve bibled my humiliations, made saints of boysin bad lighting, never considered heaven, only good weather.But since all my dead have been called home by different gods,I know they’re not, like I imagined, all waiting in the same placefor me. For so long, I thought I could get through by throwingmy faith in the general direction of any pulpit.Thank you friends for showing me your gods,& thank you gods for showing me my friends,but the heaven I choose is a heaven I can leave.

This is drawn from “Staying Still.”

title: How a Cowboy Rides When the Range is on Fire
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
When Rhonda MacDonald put out a plea for help on Facebook, the cowboys answered. Wildfires have been ravaging British Columbia, Canada, this summer—and when a ranch is put under evacuation, it is no easy feat to round up 150 free‑roaming cattle. The MacDonald herd was roaming a vast, 100,000‑acre expanse of Crown rangeland above the ranch, and the people of most use were those on horseback. This exhilarating piece documents the people who came to help, and honors the skills and hard‑won knowledge needed to navigate treacherous, fire‑scarred terrain to save the herd and help a neighbour in crisis.

Before the riders headed up Mimenuh Mountain, Wayne MacDonald stood in front of a whiteboard with a red Sharpie and began drawing. Not a map, exactly. More like 50 years of memory. He sketched the ridges, draws and escape routes cattle would choose under pressure. There was one thing he kept returning to: the lack of escape routes. “As far as road, there’s one in and one out.” They knew there might come a moment when staying was no longer brave – it was reckless.

title: AI Can See Optical Illusions
content:
Long ago, back when twirling things was both an entertaining diversion and a serious mode of scientific inquiry, several researchers noticed an odd optical illusion. Spinning a white disk with a series of black lines produced colors where there weren’t any. A toymaker named Charles Benham turned the optical illusion into a toy, and Benham's Top was born. You can try it for yourself below. 

Featured Video

Over the past 200 years, scientists have continued investigating this bizarre phenomenon (now termed “subjective color”), but it’s still somewhat mysterious. The best working theory for subjective color is that it comes from feedback in our visual cortex. Our eyes feed information forward into our brains, but our brains aren’t just sitting there waiting, they’re anticipating and predicting information to fill in the gaps. It’s this feedback that results in seeing colors in moving black-and-white images (fMRI studies seem to back up this model).

After two centuries fiddling around with the Benham’s Top illusion, scientists have uncovered several strange idiosyncrasies. For starters, arcs positioned at different distances can evoke different colors, and the colors can reverse when the direction reverses. But what’s even weirder is that artificial intelligence networks can see the Benham’s Top optical illusion too, according to a new study.  

Read more: “The Illusion Machine That Teaches Us How We See”

Researchers from the ​​National Institute for Basic Biology in Japan developed an artificial neural network (ANN) designed to predict “what image will come next” and spit out a visual representation. They trained their ANN on a series of first-person videos of natural landscapes (for example, video shot on a head-mounted GoPro from someone taking a relaxing hike). These videos, researchers say, give the network the same sort of visual training input a real person might have.  

After the training, they showed their ANN Benham’s Top, and the images it produced also included faint colors. In fact, when they tweaked the spinning disk to move the arcs or reverse the direction, the ANN “saw” the same things a human would. 

According to the team, the artificial neural network had learned to work in the same way our biological neural networks do. Because rapidly moving objects are especially challenging for the ANN to predict, they have an outsized impact during its training. The result is a “visual cortex” that works remarkably like our own, complete with the same feedback. Basically, it’s more confirmation for the feedback model of subjective color.

Benham’s Top gets a new spin, nearly 200 years later.
